title: Ezekiel 34:1–10
context: The LORD tells the prophet to prophesy against “the shepherds of Israel”, the leaders who were meant to care for the people. They “feed themselves” instead of the flock: they take the fat and the wool, but they have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the broken, brought back the driven away, or sought the lost, and they have ruled “with force and with rigor” (34:2–4). The sheep are scattered because “there was no shepherd” and become prey (34:5–6). The LORD swears that he is “against the shepherds” and will “require my sheep at their hand,” delivering his sheep from their mouth (34:7–10). The shepherd image for rulers is common in the Old Testament and its world; compare Jeremiah 23:1–4, each in its own setting. Both traditions read the chapter as an indictment of leaders who exploit those in their care, and as shared ground about the LORD’s ownership of his flock.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to me, saying”. Arminian readers note that this oracle, like the others after the news of 33:21, is spoken to a people now facing the full consequences of their leaders’ failure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD initiating a new word about the leadership of his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the formula as grounding the indictment that follows in the LORD’s authority, not in the prophet’s own grievance.

verses.text: “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy, and tell them, even the shepherds, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep?
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep?” Arminian readers note that the leaders are judged by the purpose of their office. Leadership is a trust held for the good of the flock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the shepherds as the rulers and leaders of Israel, accountable to the LORD who owns the flock. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as defining the office by service, and both apply it soberly to anyone given oversight of God’s people.

verses.text: You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: “You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep.” Arminian readers note the picture of leaders who take every benefit of their position and give nothing back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see exploitation named plainly, with the flock treated as a resource rather than a charge. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of self-serving leadership, without forcing a doctrinal fork from the image.

verses.text: You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.
verses.arminianNotes: “You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken.” Nor have they sought “that which was lost”. Arminian readers note the list of neglected duties, each showing what true care would have done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a portrait of the shepherd’s proper work drawn by its absence, and they note that the LORD will do these very things in 34:16. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge “you have ruled over them with force and with rigor” as the opposite of shepherding.

verses.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd. They became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
verses.arminianNotes: “They were scattered, because there was no shepherd. They became food to all the animals of the field”. Arminian readers note that the scattering of the people is traced to failed leadership, even as the people bear their own guilt elsewhere in the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the leaders held responsible for the flock’s ruin, without cancelling the people’s own accountability (compare 34:17–22). Shared ground: both traditions read the scattering in light of the exile, as the result of the shepherds’ neglect.

verses.text: My sheep wandered through all the mountains and on every high hill. Yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth. There was no one who searched or sought.”
verses.arminianNotes: “My sheep wandered through all the mountains and on every high hill.” Arminian readers note that the LORD calls them “my sheep” even in their scattering. “There was no one who searched or sought”, which prepares for the LORD’s own searching in 34:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the LORD’s claim of ownership over a scattered flock, which grounds his promise to seek them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament over the people’s lostness and as setting up the reversal of 34:11–16.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word:
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word”. Arminian readers note that the leaders are summoned to hear, just as the people were. No office places anyone beyond the reach of the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD calling the rulers to account before his word. Shared ground: both traditions read the summons as the transition from indictment to sentence, and both see leaders as answerable to the LORD for those in their care.

verses.text: “As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “surely because my sheep became a prey, and my sheep became food to all the animals of the field, because there was no shepherd, and my shepherds didn’t search for my sheep, but the shepherds fed themselves, and didn’t feed my sheep,
verses.arminianNotes: “As I live,” says the Lord GOD, the sheep “became a prey” because “there was no shepherd,” and “the shepherds fed themselves, and didn’t feed my sheep”. Arminian readers note that the LORD’s oath gathers up the charges of 34:2–6 into one verdict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s oath confirming the seriousness of the charges, with repeated stress on “my sheep.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the flock belongs to the LORD, so harm done to it is an offense against him.

verses.text: therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word!”
verses.arminianNotes: “therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word!” Arminian readers note that the summons is repeated before the sentence, giving weight to what follows. The repetition presses the leaders to listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the repeated call as solemn emphasis before the LORD declares his judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a rhetorical pause that heightens the sentence of 34:10.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require my sheep at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the sheep. The shepherds won’t feed themselves any more. I will deliver my sheep from their mouth, that they may not be food for them.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require my sheep at their hand”. Arminian readers note that the LORD removes the false shepherds and promises, “I will deliver my sheep from their mouth”. The flock’s rescue begins with the removal of its exploiters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD taking his flock back from unfaithful rulers and making them answer for it. Shared ground: both traditions read the language of requiring “at their hand” as recalling the watchman’s accountability in 33:6, and both see the verse as turning to the LORD’s own shepherding.
